items.title: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed
items.summary: Hundreds of millions of Indians communicate with digital systems in romanized Latin characters -- typing "aap kaise hain" rather than native script -- yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. We demonstrate that automatic metrics (BGE-M3, BERTScore) systematically misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada generation. We evaluate four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on a 12-point rubric, whereas their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004. Two distinct model-specific failure modes emerge: Gemini produces script spillage (16.9% of Telugu responses leak native script), while Qwen collapses to English-only output (16.2% of Kannada responses). We introduce a failure-aware evaluation policy that assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses, and instruction collapses -- revealing failures metrics alone cannot detect. Our results show that evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle: semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.

items.title: llm-anthropic 0.31
items.summary:
Release: llm-anthropic 0.31 
 Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. Fable 5.2 is currently ranked first on Artificial Analysis . Anthropic say it "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes", so clearly their internal benchmarks have become more ambitious! 
 I've added the new models to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this: 
 uv tool install llm
llm install llm-anthropic
llm keys set anthropic
# paste key here
llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle"
 
 I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh : 
 
 max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine. 
 It's priced at $8/million input and $40/million output, which is a 20% discount on the previous Fable 5.1 ($10/$50). 
 I also used Fable 5.2 to help identify the source of a mysterious beep . 
 
 
 Tags: llm , anthropic , claude , generative-ai , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
items.summary:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember 
Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: 
 
 [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. 
 
 For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. 
 The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others:

 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. 
 For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. 
 
 And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: 
 
 The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: 
 
 It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. 
 
 (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) 
 Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. 
 Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: 
 
 The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember.

items.title: AuthGateBench: Benchmarking LLMs as Authorization Gate
items.summary: Automated approval systems let coding agents execute high-risk actions with minimal human oversight by delegating the authorization decision to a classifier, typically a large language model (LLM). Such systems, adopted in tools like Claude Code and Codex, remain vulnerable to failure modes such as scope escalation, where the agent takes actions exceeding what the user authorized. Existing benchmarks focus mainly on malicious requests, evaluating refusal under an implicit policy. We introduce AuthGateBench, the first policy-guided benchmark for authorization gating under benign requests. We implement a novel pipeline where an LLM generates contrast pairs with identical action and trajectory but differing request, flipping the label between block and allow. This allows us to assess whether models reason over context rather than the action alone. We further examine whether auxiliary environment signals can help models make better decisions. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,400 instances spanning five failure modes drawn from real-world Claude Code incidents. Evaluations show accuracy degrades unevenly across failure modes as models over-rely on internal safety alignment, and models still block most actions even when explicitly authorized, revealing unstable rather than deterministic decisions; retrospectively retrieved environment signals, however, substantially improve authorization accuracy.
